Evacuation of intensive care units during disaster: learning from the Hurricane Sandy experience (DMPHP 2016)

dedupe_keys.name: hurricane sandy 2012 new york city hospital evacuations icu evacuation and citywide patient surge

description: This case brings together two studies of what happened to New York City hospitals when Hurricane Sandy forced several of them to evacuate patients, including the critically ill, in October 2012. Adalja and colleagues interviewed 71 key staff at the four hospital systems that received most evacuated patients, and King and colleagues surveyed 68 nurses, respiratory therapists and physicians who evacuated intensive care units at four hospitals. The producers are the author teams, publishing in Annals of Emergency Medicine (2014) and Disaster Medicine and Public Health Preparedness (2016). Coverage is New York City hospitals during and after the storm. Receiving hospitals struggled with prolonged surge, more methadone and dialysis patients, displaced staff, evacuated nursing homes, shelters already full and reimbursement; ICU evacuations lacked drills (21 percent had drilled in two years), consistent prioritisation and tracking, and reliable communication, the most cited barrier. Access is through the journals; abstracts are free on Europe PMC and the articles are behind publisher paywalls. Caveats: both are qualitative, self-reported studies without released data, and they do not give patient counts per hospital. Simulation uses: designing patient transfer and surge scenarios for hospital network models, and parameters for evacuation time and staffing constraints. Related records: the Hurricane Irene evacuation by North Shore-LIJ (case_study-hurricane-irene-nslij-hospital-evacuation) happened a year earlier in the same region.
